messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Marcus

Marcus was seventy-nine years old when he finally walked into the clinic, and the warehouse job he'd held for thirty-seven years had just ended. The tremor in his hands during the intake appointment wasn't from age alone. Sixty-eight years earlier, in rural Nigeria, he had been nine years old, playing in the tall grasses behind his family's compound while his parents argued inside. He remembered fragments: his father's voice rising, a bottle breaking, his mother's cry. He had run toward the house, then stopped at the threshold. The door—he could still feel the shock of it slamming shut in his face, though the image itself remained elusive, as if his mind had recorded the sound but erased the picture. What remained was the feeling: terror, helplessness, a certainty that something catastrophic was unfolding on the other side of that barrier. He did not see what happened next. He never quite knew what he had been spared from knowing.

The trauma had never fully surfaced until his sixties, when retirement loomed and the structure that had held him began to crack. Before that, Marcus had built a life on motion. He worked the night shift at the distribution warehouse in Newark, loading and unloading trucks in the controlled fluorescence of the industrial bay. He drank steadily—a beer at lunch, whiskey in the evenings, sometimes more. He cultivated a reputation as a friendly man, always organizing the crew for after-work gatherings, always talking, always ensuring there was noise and company around him. His marriage had ended twenty years ago; his ex-wife had said she never felt she really knew him, that he was always performing, always somewhere else even when he was right there. He had not argued the point.

But in the last three years, something had shifted. The triggers had begun to organize themselves into a pattern that Marcus could not quite name. When his nephew invited him to a family reunion at a state park upstate—a natural setting with open fields and trees—Marcus had felt an inexplicable dread. He accepted anyway, determined not to show weakness, but the moment he stepped out of the car and saw the sprawling green, something in his chest seized. He was back in that compound, waiting for something terrible. He'd made an excuse and left after an hour. That night, he drank heavily and picked a fight with his nephew over nothing, some trivial comment about the food, and it had escalated into a confrontation that left him feeling simultaneously relieved and ashamed.

The door slamming had become unbearable. At the warehouse, the loading bay doors would hydraulically close with a metallic bang, and Marcus would flinch violently, his body flooded with that old terror. His supervisor had noticed. The smell of alcohol—not just from his own drinking, but the sharp, acrid scent that sometimes drifted from a coworker or lingered on someone's breath—would trigger the same overwhelming wave of emotion without image, a tsunami of feeling that had no face attached to it. He could not remember the specifics of what had happened that day in Nigeria, could not summon a coherent narrative even when he tried, but his body remembered. The emotions came in full force, disconnected from any clear recollection.

When the triggers fired, Marcus reached for his maladaptive strategies like lifelines. A door would slam, or he would catch the scent of whiskey, and the fragmented pieces of memory—the sound, the terror, the sense of helplessness—would begin to surface. To push them back down, he would drink more, or he would engineer some small conflict with a coworker, something to argue about, to focus on, to externalize the chaos churning inside. The arguments gave him a temporary sense of agency, a way to direct the overwhelming emotion outward. He also ensured he was never alone. He would call people, invite himself to gatherings, stay late at the warehouse socializing with the crew. The constant company was a buffer against the intrusive emotions, a way to keep his mind occupied so that the disconnected memories—the fragments that would not cohere into a story—could not fully surface.

Yet these very strategies seemed to deepen the problem. The drinking, which had always been part of his life, now carried the scent of alcohol on his own breath and clothes, making him a trigger to himself. The arguments he created, while temporarily distracting, left him isolated; coworkers began to avoid him. The constant socializing exhausted him and prevented the genuine connection he actually craved. When the warehouse let him go—officially due to restructuring, but he knew his increasingly volatile behavior had played a role—the structure that had held him for nearly four decades collapsed. Without the job, without the forced social contact, without the constant motion, Marcus was left alone with the fragments and the emotions they generated. He had come to the clinic because his niece had insisted, and because he was terrified that without some intervention, he would drink himself to death before he understood what he was running from.
